events.text: The morning you rise to Upper God, every Dao you hold leans the same way, like grass in a wind from one side. At the far end of that leaning there is a place where they stop. The old gods do not talk about it. They call it the Edge of the Dao, when they call it anything.

choices.text: Go and look at it from the last domain, and come back

effects.log: You stand at the border of the last domain for a day. Past it the light thins into a colour you have no name for. You come back knowing the way.

choices.text: Ask the oldest god at the long table what it is

effects.log: The oldest god pours you nectar and says nothing for an hour. Then: "Every god who went there was stronger than me. I am still here." The table goes quiet after that.

choices.text: Turn every Dao you hold the other way, and keep it there

effects.log: It takes a season to stop listening to the lean. Your domain is calmer for it, and so are you.

events.text: You rise to Upper God, and the leaning of the Daos is not news to you. Your soul has stood at the Edge of the Dao before, more than once, and the place where it thinned is still there in your hands like the cold of a stone. Somewhere past the last domain, something remembers you too.

choices.text: Go and stand at the place where it gave

effects.log: You do not push. You only stand there, the way one stands at a grave. The nothing is a hair thinner than your soul remembers.

choices.text: Tell no god what your soul remembers

effects.log: You keep it the way the old gods keep everything: by never saying it. They notice anyway. A god who knows where they are going walks differently.

choices.text: Light a lamp in your temple for the lives that ended there

effects.log: Your priests do not ask whose lamp it is. They keep it lit all year, and it burns without oil.

events.text: A god with no temples left comes to your domain at dusk and sits on the steps. Their name has worn off every altar in the world. "You will hear it calling now," they say. "The Edge. I went. It did not want me." They are thin as smoke, and still smiling.

choices.text: Ask what it was like

effects.log: "Like a river at a cliff with no bottom," they say. "It goes on, past the end. I could see it go on." They leave before dawn. Your domain keeps their footprints for a year.

choices.text: Give them a place on your altar

effects.log: You set their old name beside your own. Your worshippers pray to both, a little puzzled. The thin god gets a little less thin.

choices.text: Send them on their way politely

effects.log: They go, still smiling. Later you find you cannot stop thinking of the river that goes on past the cliff.

events.text: A god of the Throne of Storms walks out past the last domain at noon, with the whole long table watching from the terraces. The thunder follows them as far as it can and then stops, as if at a door. The god does not come back. Their temples go dark one by one, all that week.

choices.text: Sit in one of their dark temples, so it is not empty

effects.log: Their worshippers find a stranger god on the altar and pray anyway. It is the kindest thing anyone does that week.

choices.text: Watch the place where the thunder stopped

effects.log: You watch until night. Something past the last domain flickers once, the colour of a storm, and is gone. You know the place now.

choices.text: Take their empty seat at the long table

effects.log: Nobody stops you. Nobody speaks to you either, for a long time.

events.text: An old harvest god of the Green Assembly leaves a letter on the long table and goes to the Edge of the Dao. The letter says only: "Somebody has to break it. It will not be me. But every god who falls there makes it thinner for the next." The gods pass it hand to hand in silence.

choices.text: Keep the letter

effects.log: You keep it in your domain, under a stone that never gets wet. On bad nights you read it again.

choices.text: Read it aloud at the next feast

effects.log: The pantheons hear it in your voice. A few gods stand when you finish. Most stay seated, and look at their cups.

choices.text: Burn it, before it calls anyone else

effects.log: The ash goes up the wrong way, toward the Edge. You tell yourself you saw nothing.

events.text: Past the Edge of the Dao the rules of the world go on, thin as threads, written in a hand older than the gods. Nothing lives here. Nothing has to. Behind you every pantheon is on its feet, and every lamp in every temple is burning at once.

choices.text: Walk on alone, as far as the threads go

effects.log: You walk until the threads are too thin to read, and read them anyway. When you come back the gods say you were gone a day. It was longer.

choices.text: Hold the opening for the gods who follow

effects.log: You stand in the opening for a whole season. Seven gods come through it, frightened and laughing. None of them will ever forget whose hand it was.

choices.text: Close it behind you, gently

effects.log: Some things should be found, not given. You close it the way you would close a book you love. The pantheons are angry for a century, and then grateful.

events.text: Beyond the Edge there is a single seat, carved from nothing, facing the way back. Someone sat in it once, long before the first god. The seat is warm. On its arm, in a script that is barely a script, is a word you somehow know is your name.

choices.text: Sit in the seat and look back at the world

effects.log: From the seat every domain is a lamp, and every lamp is small. You understand the gods for the first time. It is not a comfortable thing.

choices.text: Leave it empty

effects.log: You bow to the seat and leave it for whoever comes next. On the way back you feel lighter, as if you had put something down.

choices.text: Carry the word on its arm back with you

effects.log: You carry the word home and write it over the door of your temple. Gods come from every pantheon to read it. None of them can.

events.text: A century after you crossed the Edge of the Dao, young gods still come to your domain to look at your hands, as if the trick were in the fingers. A goddess of the river asks you straight out how it is done.

choices.text: Tell the truth: it took many lives, and every one ended there

effects.log: She is quiet for a long time. Then she thanks you, and does not go. Of all the answers, that one saved the most gods.

choices.text: Show her the place where it gave

effects.log: You take her to the Edge and show her. She goes back to her river with something in her face that was not there before.

choices.text: Smile, and say nothing at all

effects.log: The legend grows a little each time you say nothing. By the next feast they say you crossed it in a single breath.

events.text: At the long table a god of the oldest pantheon looks at you for a long time and says, "You have the hands of the one who crossed the Edge." You have never been there in this life. Your hands, under the table, know the cold of it anyway.

choices.text: Say it was another god, long ago

effects.log: "It was," they agree, "and it was you." Neither of you says anything more. The table, which heard, is very polite to you after that.

choices.text: Ask what that god found there

effects.log: They tell you about the seat that faces the way back, and the threads written in an older hand. It sounds like something you have forgotten, not something you have heard.

choices.text: Leave the table early

effects.log: You walk home the long way, past the last domain, and do not look toward the Edge. It looks toward you.

events.text: Your priests find an old tablet buried under your altar, from a temple that stood on this ground ages ago. It names a god who crossed the Edge of the Dao, and the prayer under the name is the one your worshippers already pray to you, word for word.

choices.text: Set the tablet back on the altar

effects.log: Your worshippers kneel to it without being told. The prayers come in a little warmer after that.

choices.text: Keep it in your own rooms

effects.log: You read the name every night until it stops being a stranger. One night it answers.

choices.text: Bury it again, deeper

effects.log: Some lives should stay lived. You bury it where the priests will not dig, and you sleep well for a hundred years.
